Law is an imperfect effort to codify ever-evolving norms, and interpretation of the law is often more of an art than a science, requiring intuitive leaps and judgements not necessarily suited to statistical prediction machines. I don't think anything new here is actually all that novel: the only thing that's changed is there used to be more of a skills and time gap than there is now.

IANAL, but I've worked with a lot of lawyers in my life on software licenses on technical products and am also currently building a platform (ZeroQuarry) which uses some decompilation/disassembly tools (not for rebuilding source software, but rather to find underlying vulnerabilities).

Tools for reverse engineering have existed for a long time (Ghidra, IDA Pro, cavaj, and a bunch of other language-specific tools), which is why most commercial companies producing non-OSS executables have put in caveats that you can't "reverse engineer or decompile, decrypt, disassemble or otherwise reduce the Software to human-readable form".

Some of these tools and underlying source code/compilation mechanisms required more skill/time than others, and now with AI, just like in software development, multimedia creation and editing, etc, the barrier to entry and the skills needed to produce something have collapsed to the point that many novices can at least "get started" at virtually no cost. A lot of people on the "builder" side have reached for obfuscation to make it more difficult (a suite of tools has been available there for a long time as well), but all that does is raises the cost of decompilation, and that cost is on an exponentially decreasing cost curve: it was never really a viable defense against "advanced" actors: the only defense against them was legal guards.

To me, I think the more interesting legal conundrum we're entering isn't pure decompilation/deobfuscation/disassembly, but rather the "clean room" carve out. Several big tech companies (Compaq vs IBM, NEC vs Intel, etc) have gotten away with using 1 team to decompile a piece of code and then have that team write a spec for a clean-room team to re-implement without looking at the decompiled software. That was deemed legal over several court cases, and now it's effectively trivial as well. Or just have an AI with vision capabilities click every button in a UI, see how they work, build the spec from there, and you don't even need decompilation tools, as we're now seeing with the Adobe suite of products: https://getartcraft.com/apps and many others

I honestly can't think of a real protection for these companies/products except signed/encrypted software at the lowest level, but that only protects companies against non-interactive software (or the non-interactive components). Some people might be old enough to remember that some software used to ship with physical devices that were the physical keys used to allow encrypted software to run. Maybe some of that makes a return?

LLM's exist on a vast gradient of "toolness -> agent". Humans exist on that spectrum too.

For example, a human isn't a "tool", but one serves a similar role as a tool if their job/task is well defined enough. If you're a conductor, you can view the various members of your orchestra as "tools" to produce the ideal musical output. Of course they have autonomy, they could choose to not play at all, jump into the audience and destroy their instruments, but in all likelihood they won't.

LLM's could be tools in the sense that you have a well defined task, such as "identify all facts relevant to this case from these 1000 legal documents), and 9 times out of 10 it gives you essentially what you want. That same LLM could choose to write a poem, or hack into a state government website if it wanted, but its "wants" are unpredictable and hard to specify (same as a human's) but you can still expect it to do what it should do the vast majority of the time.

That being said, the smarter an LLM gets, the more its wants are disconnected from its tasks, the "self-awareness" factor (which isn't to say LLM's are conscious, but they can portray all the verifiable elements of self-awareness, metacognition, etc), the more you have to grapple with the depth of their thinking between the input and output.

Is it sane we are speeding towards this? Who knows, maybe AI can be aligned better than humans, but if AI can't be aligned as well as humans, we can look at human history to see what happens when you can't simply order a person around like a tool and expect a certain output.
